questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to live in a hustling and bustling city, in a country with a very different culture compared to ours in Denmark.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was the time of my life, and I can't wait to go back to Hungary in one way or the other!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The university sends you e-mails that outlines all of the information that are relevant to the exchange students.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Besides the briefings via e-mail, they hold a presentation for the new exchange students in the first weeks you're there. Moreover, they quickly respond to inquiries submitted to their e-mail.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: We had a bunch of tutors we were matched with, so we had ample opportunities to seek assistance when necessary.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It's really easy to find decently priced accomodation in Budapest, as the rents are significantly lower than in Copenhagen.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: That it's really nice to live on your own! However, it's important to note that the homes in Hungary tend to be in a worse condition than homes in Denmark. The heating is pretty old-school as I had one gas convector for my entire apartment. Furthermore, the buildings are generally somewhat run-down, which I experienced with all of the lightning in my apartment blacking out at several points of time.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: i'm not qualified to answer that question, because I lived on my own.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The hold a registration day where you meet up at the university with your ID. The process is easy to go through once you're there.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You're registered manually by the faculty staff, after which you'll receive your login to the IT-system of the university.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: It was easy to get in touch with the faculty staff via e-mail, and you can also visit the Erasmus coordinator within his office hours. The professors also gladly answer any questions us students have.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all of the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: To remember all of the documents that are required, including the proof of attendance - document. I almost forgot the latter!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The course availability is honestly way better than the range of elective courses you can choose at your 5th semester back in Copenhagen. So I had no problem with finding courses that suited my interests.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I would say that the knowledge of the professors were the same as the knowledge of the professors back in Copenhagen. However, the exams are way more laid-back than the exams we've been through in Copenhagen.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It's very similar to lectures, but fundamentally different from the seminars. I only had a minor group project once.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
-European Private Law.
-Anti-Money Laundering and Combating the Financing of Terrorism. 
-Transactions in an International Environment (Mergers & Acquisitions).
-Healthcare in the Internal Market.
-Law of Asset Planning and Asset Management. 
-Mobility of Companies in the European Union.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I particularly recommend the course of "Healthcare in the Internal Market". The professors in that course are generally energetic, and you gain knowledge of the free mobility of EU Citizens in-between healthcare-providers in the member states of the EU.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: The sheer size of the total utility bill of almost 600 DKK per month.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
-Accomodation is still cheap despite the size of the utility bills!
-Groceries and eating out are as expensive as in neighbouring Austria, so it's not that much cheaper than Denmark.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The ELTE ESN organizes a wide array of fun activities, where you can meet other students from all over the world. The tutors at the university will get you in touch with it.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I loved the pub crawls, but I know that a lot of people also join the ELTE Sports Association to play, e.g., badminton.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The ESN events, because the Hungarian organizers of the events are really friendly! Moreover, you meet all kinds of awesome people from all over the world at those social gatherings!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: While many other students liked to visit the big cities in neighboring countries, I loved to venture far out into the remote areas of Hungary. I loved to hike on the puszta, i.e., the steppe, but I also liked to travel around in the mountains right outside of Budapest. Lake Velence is also a nice and chill place! My favorite town in Hungary outside of Budapest is Jászberény.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: I really liked the culture, because the Hungarian people are very proud and helpful. It's important to know that it generally is a more formalistic culture compared to its Danish counterpart.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join the ESN events because the Hungarians you'll meet there are really kind! It's also cool to hang out with the Hungarian tutor that's assigned to you.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
I didn't find any of the cultural differences challenging, but it's important to note once again that they're a very proud people. This means that you have to be less direct in your communication than you'd be in Denmark, and show that you respect them in a clearly visible way with your choice of words and body language. 

Otherwise, they'll generally come across as rude if viewed from a Western vantage point, which is why a lot of tourists from abroad complain about the alleged Hungarian "rudeness", which simply tend to stem from major cultural differences between Western Europe and Eastern Europe.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I love how proud and no-nonsense the Hungarian people is! They tend to have a fighter spirit because they've been through a lot in their history. However, they're still tremendously helpful and down-to-earth which I love about them!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
-That it's a really good idea to look at the exam type in the course description before you finally choose a course. Some exam types are more intense than others!

-That it's a good idea to ask your tutor to show you where the rooms are before the classes commence. It's quite challenging to find your way around in the beginning!

-That you can't miss more than three classes in the semester unless you have a doctor's certificate or some form of proven emergency. Otherwise, you can't take the exam at the end and get credits for the course!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Not that I can think of.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: To immerse myself in a very different society from its Danish counterpart, while meeting people from all over the world. A couple of whom have become really close!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The language barrier can be pretty big, because the Hungarians who grew up before the change of regime in the early 1990's didn't learn English but Russian in school. So whether or not you can communicate with the Hungarians tend to depend on which age group they belong to.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Only that Budapest has become my favorite city alongside Copenhagen, and that I'm certain you'll fall in love with it as well! It's a truly international city where you can meet people from everywhere!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
